text: Last lesson split the single-GPU problem into two pieces: not enough memory, and not enough time. This lesson is about the two different fixes — data parallelism and model parallelism — and why they're not interchangeable.

Data parallelism is the simpler case. Every GPU holds a complete, identical copy of the model, and the training data is split into shards — each GPU trains its own copy on a different batch, independently. The catch is that after each backward pass, every GPU has computed slightly different gradients from its own data, and those have to be reconciled before any weight update happens. That's AllReduce: gradients are summed across every GPU and the result is broadcast back, so every replica applies the exact same update and stays identical. The requirement underneath all of it: the model has to fit, gradients and optimizer state included, on a single GPU.

Model parallelism exists for the other case — the model itself doesn't fit, no matter how small the batch. Instead of copying it everywhere, it gets cut into pieces. Tensor parallelism cuts within a layer: a weight matrix is split across GPUs, each computing part of the same matrix multiply, with partial results combined to produce the full layer output. Pipeline parallelism cuts across layers instead — one GPU holds layers one through eight, the next holds nine through sixteen, and data flows through stage by stage, broken into micro-batches so no stage sits idle waiting.

These aren't competing options so much as tools for different jobs. Tensor parallelism needs very fast GPU-to-GPU communication, because it's synchronizing inside every single layer — that makes it best suited to GPUs on the same machine. Pipeline parallelism only communicates at stage boundaries, so it tolerates slower links between machines far better.

Real large-scale training combines all three at once — data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism together, what practitioners call three-D parallelism, implemented in frameworks like Megatron-LM and DeepSpeed. None of the three replaces the others; each solves a different piece of the memory-and-time problem. Next lesson gets into exactly why the communication side of this — the interconnect and the network topology it runs on — ends up mattering as much as the GPUs themselves.
